extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, law students, and inventors drafting or litigating patents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the required contents, form, and legal effect of patent specifications and claims — what must be described and claimed, how claims limit patent scope, and rules for framing and construing claims. Useful for drafting applications and for evaluating patent validity/scope in litigation or prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification: two principal purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The specifications are required for two principal purposes: first to inform the public what the thing is of which the patentee claims to be the inventor; and, secondly, to enable the public, after the expiration of the patent, to practise the invention from the specification, as therein described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification must both identify the invention and enable practice after expiration. (Forbes v. Barstow Stove Co. (1864) citation and related authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / full, clear, exact description
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the invention in such full, clear, and exact terms as to enable persons of competent skill in the art to reproduce the thing described from the description given in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the description is sufficient is generally a question of fact (jury in common-law cases). Courts may declare patents void if the specification is so incomplete or unintelligible as to be useless for public information. Examples/cases cited: numerous (Page v. Ferry, Reutgen v. Eanowers, Neilson v. Harford, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must conclude with specific and distinct claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute and Patent Office rules require that the specification shall conclude with a specific and distinct Claim or Claims of every separate subject-matter that the applicant desires to protect by the patent for which he has applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is no Claim there is no application (Ex parte Lasscell, Ex parte Holt). The rules of the Patent Office prescribe the concluding claim(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim: function — defines limits of exclusive use
rubrics_metrics.description: The office of the Claim is to define the limits of that exclusive use which is secured to the inventor by the patent, and thus to draw the line between those arts or instruments that are open to the public and those forbidden until patent expiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Claim is an essential part of the specification; without it one of the two great purposes of the specification is unfulfilled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim is the life of the patent and measure of privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claim is the life of the patent so far as the rights of the inventor are concerned, and by it the letters-patent, as a grant of an exclusive privilege, must stand or fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims determine the scope and identity of patents; a patent must be limited to the invention covered by its Claim. (Citations: Railroad Co. v. Mellon, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be particularly pointed out and distinctly claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor shall 'particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention or discovery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory requirement relieves courts from reconstructing the invention from a laborious history-of-the-art inquiry; the Patent Office examines and scrutinizes the Claim. (Statutory language cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims construed strictly; courts will not enlarge claim by description
rubrics_metrics.description: When the terms of a Claim in the letters-patent are explicit, the courts cannot alter or enlarge it; the court will not go into the history of the art to expand a Claim beyond its language or allow it to be enlarged by the Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patentees have not claimed the whole of their invention, they should correct by surrender and reissue; courts take patentees at their word. (Keystone Bridge Co. v. Phoenix Iron Co., James v. Campbell.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence or insufficiency of Claim defeats relief
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Claim does not define the invention, the courts can give no relief; where there is no Claim there is no application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and Patent Office decisions (Delaware Coal & Ice Co. v. Packer et al.) emphasize that an insufficient Claim prevents enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed matter: exclusion, abandonment, or postponement
rubrics_metrics.description: All matters not claimed are considered as excluded from the particular invention. Failure to claim described matter may admit it to be old or may be an abandonment to the public, but these statements require qualification — omission does not automatically dedicate new matter unless intent or public use/sale indicates abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor may describe but reserve other inventions for future patents (must expressly reserve). Claiming one specific device and omitting others apparent in the specification can be an abandonment of the latter unless inadvertence, reissue, etc. (cases cited: Swift v. Jenks, Miller v. Brass Co., Combined Patents Can Co. v. Lloyd, Ex parte Roberts, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must set forth a practically operative means / usable invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Claim must set forth and claim a practically operative means. The inventor must at least describe and claim some art or instrument capable of practical use; nothing less is a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Claim may be narrow if it covers an operative means. Claims for devices that under some circumstances would not operate can still be proper. (Ex parte Cornell, American Pin Co., Wheeler v. Clipper Mower & Reaper Co., Ex parte Emerson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must be for a concrete art or instrument (not abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Claim must be for a concrete invention; patents are not granted for abstract ideas or scientific theories but for practical arts, mechanisms, or products available for use on physical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The thing patented is the concrete expression (the art, mechanism, or product) in which the idea is reduced to practice. (Ex parte DesignoUe, Burr v. Duryee, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must be confined to a single and distinct invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Claim must be confined to some single and distinct invention; two arts or instruments cannot be embraced in one Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where general inventions admit substantially different modifications, each distinct idea must be claimed separately. Process and product, machine and product, etc., generally cannot be combined in one Claim. (Opinion Atty. Gen. (1856), Ex parte Bland, Ex parte Bates.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must indicate the class of invention (art, machine, manufacture, composition, design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Claim must define the invention in a manner that indicates to which class of patentable inventions it belongs (art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, design, or improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Claim need not state the class explicitly, but it must be apparent; e.g., if the real invention is an art/process it must be claimed as such and not as the product or the means. (Ex parte Mayall, Hatch v. Moffitt, Burr v. Daryee.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must precisely define the exact limits of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Claim must precisely define the exact limits of the invention claimed, either by enumeration of essential characteristics or by such delineation of the invention as identifies it with the one described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the invention is a complete art or instrument, it must be claimed as such without reference to purposes; when only parts are new, the Claim must state the new parts. Elements implied by the Claim may be read in where the device is useful only as part of a whole. (Ex parte Thompson, Seymour v. Osborne, Ex parte West.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim mode of operation or objects when invention is concrete
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention is a concrete art or instrument, it must be claimed as the thing itself, not as a 'mode of operation' or by reference to the objects/purposes for which it is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention is an apparatus, it must be claimed as such and not merely as a means for practicing an art. Conversely, if the invention is really a new use of a known instrument, the new use (and the objects/mode of operation) must be claimed, not the instrument itself. (Hatch v. Moffitt, Burr v. Daryee, Piper v. Brown, Merrill v. Yeomans.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must distinguish claimed invention from all known inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Claim must distinguish the art or instrument it embraces from every art or instrument already known (i.e., properly define novelty over prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Claim should express no more and no less than is necessary to convey an accurate understanding of the actual invention made; additional independent features should be claimed separately when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming one specific arrangement excludes other arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: If new devices are claimed as specifically arranged, the Claim covers them only when thus arranged; a Claim that sets forth a certain arrangement as essential will not cover other arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements described as specifically arranged are limited to that arrangement (Tate v. Thomas, Carlton v. Bokee). Conversely, elements indispensable to the invention are not covered unless mentioned in the Claim. (McMillin v. Rees.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming non-essential or auxiliary elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements not essential to the invention should not be stated in the Claim; what is described as merely auxiliary should not be claimed as essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Claim including useless things is not void unless they are claimed as essential. A Claim must not include parts/features not embraced in the intended invention. (Ex parte Skinner, Ex parte Wheat, Lewis v. — cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositions: must state operative proportions and necessary details
rubrics_metrics.description: For compositions of matter, it is insufficient to give only the names of substances to be mixed without stating any relative proportion; the specification must describe nature and extent of the improvement so the public can practise it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composition details (e.g., proportions) are omitted, court duty arises to determine sufficiency; otherwise patent may be void for incompleteness (cases: Evans v. Eaton and related authorities).
